# Constraint

- Inherits [`Instance`](instance.md)
- **Not creatable**: it cannot be created with `Instance.new`
- **Abstract**: it cannot be created; other classes inherit from it

The abstract base class of physics joints. A constraint connects two parts through two `Attachment`s, and the physics solver works out how both parts move: a door swings under its own weight, a ragdoll falls.

A constraint is not a `Weld`. A weld moves its second part with its first every tick, without the solver; use it to attach one thing to another. Use a constraint for parts that move relative to each other.

The two attachments set where the joint is on each part. A constraint cannot be connected to a `CharacterBody`, which is moved by its controller and not by the solver.

This page lists the members this class declares. Inherited members are
listed on the page of the class that declares them.

## Properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Attachment0` | `Attachment?` | — | read/write | The attachment at one end of the joint. The part it is on is one of the two bodies the joint connects. |
| `Attachment1` | `Attachment?` | — | read/write | The attachment at the other end of the joint. When the joint is created, the two attachments mark the same place on the two parts. |
| `BreakForce` | `number` | `0` | read/write | The force, in newtons, above which the joint breaks. A joint that breaks is disabled and fires `Broken`. At 0 the joint never breaks. |
| `BreakTorque` | `number` | `0` | read/write | The torque, in newton meters, above which the joint breaks. At 0 the joint never breaks. |
| `CollideConnected` | `boolean` | `true` | read/write | Whether the two connected parts collide with each other. Turn it off for parts that overlap at the joint, such as the upper and lower arm of a ragdoll, or they push each other apart every step. |
| `Enabled` | `boolean` | `true` | read/write | Whether the joint holds. A disabled constraint stays in the world and holds nothing. It keeps its place in the solver's order, so enabling it again behaves as it did before; destroying and recreating a joint does not guarantee that. |
| `Visible` | `boolean` | `false` | read/write | Whether the constraint is drawn. In the editor and in the debug overlay, every constraint is drawn as a shape that shows what it is. In a running game, only a rope, a rod and a spring are drawn, as a thin line with their `Color` and `Thickness`. |

## Methods

### `GetForce(): number`

Returns the force, in newtons, that the joint applied during the last simulation tick to hold its two parts together. This is the value `BreakForce` is compared with. Returns 0 for a constraint that only drives motion, such as `AlignPosition`; use `GetMotorForce` for those.

### `GetMotorForce(): number`

Returns the force, in newtons, that the constraint's motor applied during the last simulation tick. It applies to the actuator of a `PrismaticConstraint`, an `AlignPosition` and a `LinearVelocity`. It is separate from `GetForce`, which is the load the joint carried. Returns 0 for a constraint with no linear motor.

### `GetMotorTorque(): number`

Returns the torque, in newton meters, that the constraint's motor applied during the last simulation tick. It applies to the actuator of a `HingeConstraint` or a `BallSocketConstraint`, an `AlignOrientation` and an `AngularVelocity`. A servo that reads its `ServoMaxTorque` here is at its limit. Returns 0 for a constraint with no rotary motor.

### `GetTorque(): number`

Returns the torque, in newton meters, that the joint applied during the last simulation tick to resist turning. Returns 0 for a joint that does not resist turning, such as a ball joint or a rope.

## Events

Signals are deferred: a handler runs at the next resumption point, not
inside the call that fired the signal.

### `Broken()`

Fires when the joint breaks because it carried more than `BreakForce` or `BreakTorque`. The joint is disabled, not destroyed; set `Enabled` to true to restore it.
